section.title: The percentage of code generated is less useful than the work humans still own
section.deck: Anders Hejlsberg distinguishes growing code volume from the responsibility to understand a real system.

blocks.question: Will AI soon write more than 90 percent of code?
answer: Hejlsberg asks what the percentage measures. Some generated applications already consist entirely of AI-written code, and generation itself greatly increases the total volume. A large share of that expanding denominator is different from a large share of high-quality, novel software. He is skeptical of treating those claims as equivalent.
He expects AI to do impressive things, but does not assume that increasing success on familiar patterns establishes that it can perform every kind of engineering work.

followups.question: What is an example of code that does not fit the optimistic claim?
answer: He says his team tried using AI for their TypeScript compiler work and found it unable to reproduce that particular implementation. His explanation is that the unusual concepts and structure are not a typical match for learned patterns. He treats this as a limitation of the tools he tested, while acknowledging that they are improving. It is not a timeless claim about every future model or compiler.
followups.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.question: Could engineers stop reading the code or using an IDE?
answer: Hejlsberg worries about the point where prompting no longer fixes a bug or implements the next feature. Someone must then understand the system underneath. He also emphasizes responsibility for the application’s effects: the person or organization deploying it cannot treat AI as a substitute for understanding what they are vouching for. His hypothetical harm example illustrates that responsibility; it is not a legal determination made by this book.

followups.question: Why does your view differ from the more sweeping claims made by some AI developers?
answer: He distinguishes admiration for AI from extrapolating its contribution to complete human irrelevance. Even if generation handles a larger percentage of code, people still need to connect the system to the business problem and the organization around it. That larger context is what a simple generation percentage leaves out.
followups.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.question: Will AI replace junior engineering work?
answer: He questions how senior engineers would be developed if junior participation disappeared entirely. He thinks the entry-level pyramid may narrow for some work and people may be expected to move toward supervision more quickly. The craft can shift from typing code toward reviewing agents’ work, but he still sees programmers as part of the process. These are his expectations in the interview rather than a current employment forecast.
blocks.speaker: Anders Hejlsberg

blocks.question: Would a future with less manual coding make the work less enjoyable for you?
answer: Hejlsberg still enjoys writing code after decades of doing it, but is happy to delegate parts he finds tedious, including testing-framework boilerplate. Reviewing other people’s code has often felt harder to him than writing his own. He hopes tools can make review more understandable and ergonomic by explaining changes rather than merely displaying file lists and diffs. The transition can change the craft without making every part equally attractive to every programmer.
